messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael, a 34-year-old school counselor, had always taken pride in his ability to remain calm in a crisis. That changed one afternoon when an eighth grader who had been threatening self-harm lunged for a pair of scissors on his desk. Acting on instinct, Michael grabbed the boy’s arm and pulled him back, but the student lost his footing and crashed head-first into the corner of a filing cabinet. The sound—a sickening crack—was followed by silence, then a seizure. Michael called 911, but the boy suffered a traumatic brain injury that required weeks of hospitalization. In the months that followed, Michael’s world narrowed to that single moment.

The memory did not fade. It came back fully—the smell of the room, the warmth of the boy’s arm, the crack—as if it were happening right now, across all his senses at once. Because the memory arrived with such force, Michael started noticing his heart pound at any sharp sound—a dropped tray in the cafeteria, a car backfiring—sounds that had never troubled him before, now felt like warnings. Yet when he tried to describe it, he could only produce fragments; the words would not come. The hospital’s antiseptic smell during a routine checkup plunged him back into that room, and he felt the same panic surge through his chest. After that appointment, Michael began calling ahead to schedule visits at times when the lobby was emptiest, and he would stand outside until the last possible moment—anything to avoid the smell and the memory it unleashed. Stress from work or a minor argument with his wife made his self-blame worse: he would think, “I should have done something differently. I destroyed his life—and mine.” The more he blamed himself, the more vivid the memory became, and each reliving confirmed that his life was finished. He began to doubt that he could ever make a good decision again.

To survive, Michael kept his mind occupied all the time. He played podcasts while driving, listened to music during lunch, and stayed up late cleaning the garage. But the effort of maintaining this constant distraction exhausted him, and the memory would break through even stronger, leaving him shaking. His inability to stop the intrusions convinced him he was fundamentally broken. He started avoiding the police station on his commute—taking a longer route—and that careful avoidance made him hypervigilant for any sign of a patrol car, so that a glimpse of a squad car became a trigger in itself. At night, he could not let himself fall asleep easily; he lay rigid, listening for sounds, alert to imagined danger. That hypervigilance drove him to find even more distractions before bed, but they only left him more on edge, and his body’s racing heart often brought the memory flooding back.

Over months, the pattern tightened. Every stress—a deadline, a phone call from the district—made his self-recrimination sharper, and sharper blame made him more sensitive to new stress, creating a loop he could not escape. He stopped telling his wife about his days because each time he tried to speak, the memory returned and he could not find the words. He took leave from work, hoping rest would help, but the emptiness only gave the memory more room. What frightened him most was the thought that if he ever let himself fully think about the event, he would fall apart completely. Yet the memory pushed through anyway, and each time it did, he felt the same overwhelming guilt, the same certainty that his life was destroyed.

Finally, his wife insisted he see someone. Michael agreed, but he came to the first session terrified: terrified that talking would make the memory worse, and terrified that nothing could ever make it better. He hoped someone might quiet the memory, but deep down he feared the memory would always feel like it was happening right now.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show a causal relationship where Michael's negative appraisals (e.g., self-blame, feeling broken) directly drive his maladaptive coping strategies (avoidance, distraction); instead, these strategies appear driven by the memory and threat.

The vignette does not show a causal relationship where Michael's maladaptive strategies (e.g., distraction, avoidance) directly worsen his negative appraisals; the strategies lead to memory breakthroughs which then fuel negative appraisals.
